title: World War I: Crash Course World History
speaker: John Green
description: John Green covers the causes, major events, and lasting consequences of World War I in this fast-paced overview.
summary:
World War I, fought between 1914 and 1918, was one of the deadliest conflicts in human history. It killed approximately 17 million people and wounded another 20 million. It reshaped the map of Europe, brought down four empires, and set in motion events that would lead to World War II just two decades later.

The war began in the summer of 1914 following the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary in Sarajevo. This triggered a series of alliances that drew the major European powers into conflict. On one side were the Allied Powers — primarily Britain, France, Russia, and later the United States and Italy. On the other were the Central Powers — Germany, Austria-Hungary, and the Ottoman Empire.

The war introduced industrial-scale warfare. Machine guns, poison gas, artillery barrages, and barbed wire created a new kind of conflict in which soldiers faced each other from trenches that stretched for hundreds of kilometres. The Western Front in France and Belgium saw years of horrific stalemate, with millions of casualties for gains of just a few kilometres.

The war changed the world's political map dramatically. The Russian Revolution of 1917 brought the Bolsheviks to power and took Russia out of the war. The Ottoman Empire collapsed, leading to the creation of modern Turkey and shaping the borders of the modern Middle East. The Austro-Hungarian Empire dissolved into multiple new nations.

The Treaty of Versailles, signed in 1919, officially ended the war. It imposed harsh penalties on Germany — reparations, territorial losses, and military restrictions. Many historians argue that these conditions created the economic hardship and national humiliation that helped fuel the rise of Adolf Hitler and the outbreak of World War II.

World War I marked the end of one world order and the beginning of another — an era of mass politics, global conflict, and the decline of European imperial power.

title: World War II: Crash Course World History
speaker: John Green
description: From the rise of fascism to the atomic bomb, John Green traces the causes, events, and legacy of humanity's deadliest conflict.
summary:
World War II, fought between 1939 and 1945, was the deadliest conflict in human history. An estimated 70 to 85 million people died — the majority of them civilians. It was also the first war in which deliberate mass murder of civilians was a systematic state policy.

The war grew out of the unresolved tensions of World War I. In Germany, economic collapse after the Great Depression and the humiliation of the Versailles Treaty created conditions that allowed Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party to rise to power. Hitler's aggressive foreign policy — the annexation of Austria, the seizure of Czechoslovakia, and finally the invasion of Poland in September 1939 — triggered declarations of war from Britain and France.

The war was fought on multiple continents. In Europe, Germany achieved rapid early victories, conquering France in six weeks. Germany then turned on its former ally, the Soviet Union, in a massive invasion in 1941 that eventually cost millions of lives on both sides. Japan's attack on the American naval base at Pearl Harbor in December 1941 brought the United States into the war.

The Holocaust — the systematic genocide of six million Jewish people and millions of others, including Roma, disabled people, and political prisoners — was carried out by the Nazi regime. This industrial-scale murder, made possible by modern bureaucracy and technology, shocked the world and led directly to the development of international human rights law.

The war ended in Europe in May 1945 following Germany's surrender. In the Pacific, the United States dropped atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, killing approximately 200,000 people. Japan surrendered shortly after.

The war's legacy shaped the modern world: the United Nations, the Cold War, the State of Israel, decolonisation across Asia and Africa, and the nuclear age all emerged directly from its consequences.

title: Introduction to Psychology: Crash Course
speaker: Hank Green
description: What is psychology, and how do psychologists study the mind? Hank Green introduces the field, its history, and its main approaches.
summary:
Psychology is the scientific study of the mind and behaviour. It asks fundamental questions: Why do people act the way they do? How do emotions affect our decisions? What causes mental illness? How does memory work? These questions matter not just academically but in everyday life — in how we relate to each other, how we raise children, how we design workplaces, and how we treat psychological disorders.

Psychology as a formal science began in the late 19th century. Wilhelm Wundt opened the first psychology laboratory in Leipzig, Germany, in 1879, where he tried to study the structure of the mind through controlled experiments. Sigmund Freud, around the same time, was developing psychoanalysis — a theory that our behaviour is shaped by unconscious drives and early childhood experiences. Freud's ideas were enormously influential, though many of his specific claims have not held up to scientific testing.

In the 20th century, behaviourism — championed by psychologists like John B. Watson and B.F. Skinner — argued that psychology should focus only on observable behaviour, not on internal mental states. Skinner showed how behaviour could be shaped by rewards and punishments in a process called operant conditioning.

Cognitive psychology emerged as a challenge to behaviourism, arguing that internal mental processes — thinking, memory, attention, language — are essential to understanding behaviour. Modern neuroscience has extended this by linking mental processes to brain activity.

Today, psychology encompasses many branches: clinical psychology (treating mental disorders), social psychology (how people influence each other), developmental psychology (how the mind changes over a lifetime), and neuropsychology (the relationship between the brain and behaviour).

Psychology has produced practical insights that affect almost every aspect of modern life — from how we design advertisements and train athletes to how we understand prejudice and treat depression.

title: Supply and Demand: Crash Course Economics
speaker: Adriene Hill
description: Supply and demand is the foundation of market economics. Adriene Hill explains how prices are set and what happens when markets respond to change.
summary:
Supply and demand is one of the most fundamental concepts in economics. It explains how prices are set in markets and how economies respond to change. Understanding it is essential to making sense of economic news, business decisions, and government policy.

Demand refers to how much of a product consumers want to buy at different prices. In general, when the price of something rises, people buy less of it — this is the law of demand. When the price falls, people buy more. A demand curve on a graph slopes downward from left to right, showing this relationship.

Supply refers to how much of a product producers are willing to sell at different prices. When the price is high, sellers want to produce and sell more — this is the law of supply. A supply curve slopes upward from left to right.

Markets reach equilibrium where supply and demand intersect — the price at which the quantity supplied exactly equals the quantity demanded. At this price, there is no surplus (too much supply) and no shortage (too much demand). The market clears.

But markets are constantly changing. If consumer incomes rise, demand for goods increases — the demand curve shifts right, pushing up both price and quantity. If a new technology makes production cheaper, supply increases — the supply curve shifts right, pushing down prices. Every day, millions of such shifts occur in markets around the world.

Governments sometimes intervene in markets — setting price controls, minimum wages, or taxes. These interventions have predictable effects on supply and demand. A price ceiling (maximum price) below the equilibrium creates a shortage. A price floor (minimum price) above the equilibrium creates a surplus.

Supply and demand analysis applies far beyond grocery stores and petrol stations — to labour markets, housing, healthcare, and financial markets. It is the starting point for almost all economic analysis.

title: Natural Selection: Crash Course Biology
speaker: Hank Green
description: Charles Darwin's theory of natural selection is the foundation of modern biology. Hank Green explains how it works and why the evidence is overwhelming.
summary:
Natural selection is the mechanism that drives evolution — the process by which living things change over time. It was first described by Charles Darwin in his 1859 book On the Origin of Species, and it remains one of the most important ideas in the history of science.

The idea is elegantly simple. Individuals within a population vary — some are faster, some more resistant to disease, some better camouflaged. These differences are often inherited. Individuals that are better suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing on their advantageous traits to their offspring. Over many generations, these traits become more common in the population. This is natural selection.

Darwin arrived at his theory after years of observation, including a voyage to the Galapagos Islands, where he noticed that finches on different islands had differently shaped beaks — each adapted to the food sources available on that island. He realised that the birds had diverged from a common ancestor, with different populations adapting to different environments over time.

The evidence for evolution by natural selection is overwhelming and comes from multiple independent sources: the fossil record, comparative anatomy, genetics, and direct observation of evolution happening in real time. Bacteria evolving antibiotic resistance is natural selection in action, happening over years rather than millennia.

One common misunderstanding is that evolution has a direction or goal. It does not. Natural selection simply favours whatever traits help organisms survive and reproduce in their current environment. As environments change, what is selected for changes too.

Evolution by natural selection is the unifying theory of biology — it explains the diversity of life, the similarities between species, the structure of ecosystems, and the ongoing arms race between predators and prey, parasites and hosts, pathogens and immune systems.

title: Climate Science: Crash Course
speaker: Hank Green
description: What does the science actually say about climate change? Hank Green cuts through the noise to explain the evidence, the mechanisms, and the projections.
summary:
Climate change is one of the most important and most misunderstood topics of our time. Understanding the science — not just the politics — is essential for making sense of what is happening to our planet and what we might do about it.

The Earth's climate is determined by a balance between energy arriving from the sun and energy escaping back into space. Greenhouse gases — primarily carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapour — trap some of this outgoing energy, warming the planet. This is the greenhouse effect, and it is not a modern discovery — scientists have understood it since the 19th century. Without it, Earth would be about 30 degrees Celsius colder than it is.

The problem is that human activities — particularly burning fossil fuels — are adding extra greenhouse gases to the atmosphere faster than natural systems can absorb them. Carbon dioxide concentration in the atmosphere is now higher than at any point in the past 800,000 years, based on ice core records.

As a result, the planet is warming. The average global temperature has risen approximately 1.1 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. This may sound small, but average temperatures are averages — the actual changes at regional level can be much larger, and even small changes in global average temperature translate to large changes in weather patterns, ice cover, and sea levels.

The projections for the future depend on how much greenhouse gas we continue to emit. Under high-emission scenarios, warming of 3 to 5 degrees Celsius by 2100 is possible — a level of change that would be catastrophic for many parts of the world. Under aggressive emissions reduction, warming could be limited to 1.5 to 2 degrees.

The science is clear and the scientific consensus is overwhelming. The debate is not about whether climate change is happening or whether humans are causing it. The debate is about what to do about it — and how fast.

title: Introduction to Sociology: Crash Course
speaker: Nicole Sweeney
description: Sociology studies how society shapes individuals and how individuals shape society. Nicole Sweeney introduces the key ideas and why they matter.
summary:
Sociology is the study of human society — how it is organised, how it changes, and how it shapes the people who live within it. It asks questions that are at once deeply personal and broadly political: Why do different groups have different life outcomes? How do social norms develop and change? What holds societies together, and what tears them apart?

Sociology emerged as a formal discipline in the 19th century, when rapid industrialisation and urbanisation were transforming European society. Early sociologists like Émile Durkheim, Karl Marx, and Max Weber tried to understand these changes systematically. Durkheim studied suicide rates and discovered they varied predictably with social factors — showing that even deeply personal acts are shaped by social forces. Marx analysed how economic systems create conflict between social classes. Weber examined how culture, religion, and bureaucracy shape social life.

Sociologists use the concept of 'sociological imagination' — a term coined by C. Wright Mills — to understand how personal experiences are connected to larger social structures and historical forces. When you are unemployed, for example, it may feel like a personal failure. But if unemployment is high across society, the cause is economic and structural, not personal.

Sociology examines institutions — family, education, religion, media, law — and asks how they reproduce or challenge social inequalities. It studies how race, class, gender, and sexuality affect people's opportunities and experiences. It investigates how social norms — shared expectations about behaviour — are established and enforced.

Sociology is relevant to almost every area of public life: public health, education policy, crime, poverty, and social movements. By revealing the social structures beneath everyday life, sociology gives us tools to understand and potentially change the world we live in.

title: Hamlet: Crash Course Literature
speaker: John Green
description: John Green digs into Shakespeare's most famous tragedy — the ambiguity, the language, and the questions about revenge, mortality, and action that have kept audiences arguing for 400 years.
summary:
Hamlet is widely considered Shakespeare's greatest play and one of the most important works in the English language. Written around 1600, it tells the story of Prince Hamlet of Denmark, whose father has recently died and whose uncle Claudius has taken the throne by marrying Hamlet's mother, Gertrude. When the ghost of Hamlet's father appears and reveals that Claudius murdered him, Hamlet is called to revenge.

What makes Hamlet extraordinary is not its plot — revenge tragedies were common in Shakespeare's time — but its depth of character and ambiguity. Hamlet is intelligent, witty, philosophical, and paralysed. He famously spends much of the play thinking about action rather than taking it. His 'To be or not to be' soliloquy — the most famous speech in the English language — is a meditation on existence itself: whether it is nobler to endure life's suffering or to end it.

The play raises questions that Shakespeare deliberately leaves unanswered. Is the ghost really Hamlet's father, or a devil in disguise? Is Hamlet's madness real or performed? Is Gertrude complicit in her husband's murder? These ambiguities are not flaws — they are part of what makes the play so rich and so endlessly debatable.

Hamlet is also a play about theatre itself. The Players' scene — in which Hamlet arranges for actors to perform a play mimicking his father's murder — raises questions about the relationship between performance and truth. The play questions how we know what we know, how we tell the difference between appearance and reality.

Four hundred years after it was written, Hamlet continues to fascinate because its central questions — about grief, action, revenge, and the purpose of existence — remain urgent. It is a play that has meant different things to every generation that has staged it.

title: Introduction to Philosophy: Crash Course
speaker: Hank Green
description: What is philosophy and why does it matter? Hank Green introduces the central questions philosophers ask and why careful thinking about them is valuable.
summary:
Philosophy is the love of wisdom — the word comes from the Greek philosophia. It is the oldest academic discipline, predating modern science, and it asks questions that are at once the most basic and the most difficult: What is real? What can we know? What is right and wrong? What is the nature of the mind? What makes a just society?

These questions may seem abstract, but they underlie almost everything we do. Every time you make a moral decision, you are implicitly doing ethics — the branch of philosophy that studies right and wrong. Every time you accept or reject an argument as logical, you are applying principles of logic. Every time you ask whether something you believe is really true, you are doing epistemology — the study of knowledge.

Western philosophy is typically traced to ancient Greece. Socrates — who left no writings and is known only through the dialogues written by his student Plato — developed a method of inquiry through questioning, revealing that people's confident beliefs often rest on confused foundations. His method, the Socratic method, remains a powerful tool for critical thinking.

Plato argued that the physical world we experience is a shadow of a deeper reality of abstract forms. His student Aristotle rejected this, arguing for a more empirical approach — carefully observing the world to understand it. This tension between rationalism and empiricism runs through the history of philosophy to the present day.

Philosophy has had practical consequences. Enlightenment philosophy gave us the concepts of individual rights and democratic government. Utilitarian philosophy shaped modern public policy. Feminist philosophy challenged assumptions about who counts as a full person in public life.

Learning to think philosophically — carefully, systematically, and with awareness of assumptions — is valuable in any field and any walk of life. It teaches the discipline of thinking clearly about hard questions.

title: Globalisation: Crash Course Economics
speaker: Adriene Hill
description: Globalisation has lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty — but it has also created new inequalities and disrupted communities. Adriene Hill examines both sides.
summary:
Globalisation refers to the increasing interconnection of the world's economies, cultures, and populations. Over the past fifty years, international trade, communication, and migration have intensified to a degree unprecedented in human history. Goods, money, people, and ideas flow across borders more freely than ever before.

The economic case for globalisation rests on the principle of comparative advantage — the idea that countries benefit by specialising in what they produce most efficiently and trading for everything else. When trade barriers fall, economies can specialise, producing more at lower cost. Global supply chains, in which different stages of production occur in different countries, have made manufacturing more efficient and products cheaper.

The results have been significant. Extreme poverty has declined dramatically. According to the World Bank, the share of the world's population living in extreme poverty fell from 36 percent in 1990 to around 10 percent by 2015. Much of this improvement is concentrated in East and Southeast Asia, particularly China, where export-led industrialisation lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty.

But globalisation's benefits have been distributed unevenly. Within many wealthy countries, manufacturing workers whose jobs moved to lower-wage countries experienced unemployment and wage stagnation. Communities built around industries that relocated saw economic decline, contributing to political discontent and the rise of populist movements.

Globalisation has also raised concerns about race to the bottom — the competitive pressure on countries to attract investment by lowering environmental standards, workers' rights, and taxes. International agreements and institutions attempt to set common standards, but enforcement is difficult.

The relationship between globalisation and cultural identity is complex. The spread of global brands, media, and languages raises concerns about cultural homogenisation — the flattening of local cultures under a global monoculture. At the same time, globalisation enables cultural exchange, the spread of ideas, and hybrid cultures that blend influences from multiple traditions.

title: The Solar System: Crash Course Astronomy
speaker: Phil Plait
description: Phil Plait takes us on a tour of our solar system — from the scorching surface of Mercury to the icy reaches of the outer planets.
summary:
Our solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a cloud of gas and dust. Gravity caused the cloud to collapse, and most of the material fell to the centre to form the Sun. The remaining material formed a flat disc around the Sun, and within this disc, clumps of material began to stick together — eventually forming the planets, moons, asteroids, and comets that make up the solar system today.

At the centre is the Sun — a medium-sized star that accounts for 99.86 percent of all the mass in the solar system. The Sun is so large that about 1.3 million Earths could fit inside it. It produces energy through nuclear fusion, converting hydrogen into helium at its core.

The inner solar system contains four rocky planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. Mercury is the smallest and fastest-orbiting planet. Venus is the hottest — its thick atmosphere traps heat, raising surface temperatures to nearly 470 degrees Celsius. Earth is the only planet known to support life. Mars has the solar system's largest volcano and a canyon that dwarfs the Grand Canyon.

Beyond Mars lies the asteroid belt — a region of rocky debris left over from the formation of the solar system. Then come the gas giants: Jupiter, the largest planet; Saturn, famous for its spectacular ring system; Uranus and Neptune, the 'ice giants' — cold, windswept worlds at the edge of the solar system.

Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper Belt, a region of icy objects including Pluto — reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 — and many other small bodies. Further still is the Oort Cloud, a vast spherical shell of icy objects that is thought to be the source of long-period comets.

Our solar system is just one of hundreds of billions in the Milky Way galaxy, which is itself one of hundreds of billions of galaxies in the observable universe.

title: Media Literacy: Crash Course
speaker: Jay Smooth
description: We are surrounded by media — but how much do we think critically about what we consume? Jay Smooth introduces the tools of media literacy.
summary:
Every day, we consume enormous amounts of media — news, social media, advertising, entertainment, podcasts, videos. Media shapes what we know, what we believe, and how we see the world. But how often do we think critically about the media we consume? Media literacy is the ability to access, analyse, evaluate, and create media thoughtfully — and it is increasingly essential in the digital age.

All media is constructed. Every news article, photograph, and video involves choices — what to include, what to leave out, how to frame a story, whose perspective to represent. These choices reflect the values, assumptions, and interests of the people who made them. Recognising this is the starting point of media literacy.

Media serves many purposes: to inform, to persuade, to entertain, to sell. Advertising is perhaps the most obvious form of persuasive media — but news, political messaging, and entertainment also persuade, often in less obvious ways. Understanding who created a piece of media and what they want you to think or do is a critical first step.

In the digital age, misinformation spreads faster than ever before. Social media algorithms are designed to maximise engagement — and emotionally charged, outrageous, or divisive content tends to generate more engagement than calm, accurate reporting. This creates incentives for the production and spread of misleading information.

Fact-checking skills are essential: verifying the source of information, looking for corroboration from multiple reliable sources, checking the date of a story, and being sceptical of information that confirms what you already believe.

Media literacy also involves understanding representation — who is shown in media and how. Research consistently shows that media representation affects how different groups see themselves and are seen by others. Critically examining whose stories are told and whose are absent is part of reading media thoughtfully.

Being media literate does not mean distrusting all media — it means engaging with it actively, with awareness and critical thinking.

title: The U.S. Constitution: Crash Course Government
speaker: Craig Benzine
description: The U.S. Constitution is one of the most influential political documents in history. Craig Benzine explains how it works — and why it is so hard to change.
summary:
The United States Constitution, drafted in 1787 and ratified in 1788, is one of the most influential political documents ever written. It established the structure of the U.S. government, defined the powers and limits of each branch, and set out fundamental rights and principles that have shaped not just American law but constitutional democracy around the world.

The Constitution was written in response to the failure of the Articles of Confederation, the first governing document of the United States, which gave so little power to the central government that it could barely function. The delegates who gathered in Philadelphia in 1787 faced a fundamental challenge: how to create a government strong enough to be effective while preventing any single person or group from gaining too much power.

Their solution was a system of separation of powers and checks and balances. Power was divided among three branches: the legislative branch (Congress), which makes laws; the executive branch (the President), which enforces them; and the judicial branch (the Supreme Court), which interprets them. Each branch was given ways to limit the others — the President can veto laws passed by Congress, Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds majority, and the Supreme Court can strike down laws it finds unconstitutional.

The Constitution also divided power between the federal government and the states — a system called federalism. The Tenth Amendment reserves powers not given to the federal government to the states.

The first ten amendments to the Constitution — the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791 — protect individual freedoms: freedom of speech, religion, and the press; the right to a fair trial; protection against unreasonable searches. These rights have been interpreted, extended, and debated by the courts ever since.

Amending the Constitution is deliberately difficult — requiring approval by two-thirds of both houses of Congress and ratification by three-quarters of states. In over 230 years, only 27 amendments have been passed. This difficulty means the Constitution's original structure has remained largely intact, even as American society has changed dramatically.

title: Cells: Crash Course Biology
speaker: Hank Green
description: Every living thing is made of cells. Hank Green explains what cells are, how they work, and why cell biology is central to understanding all of life.
summary:
All living things on Earth — from bacteria to blue whales, from oak trees to humans — are made of cells. The cell is the basic unit of life. Understanding cells is understanding the foundation of biology.

The cell theory, developed in the 19th century, states three things: all living organisms are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living organisms; and all cells come from pre-existing cells. This last point — that life only comes from life — was revolutionary, finally disproving the ancient idea of spontaneous generation.

There are two fundamental types of cells. Prokaryotic cells are simpler and older — they have no nucleus or other membrane-bound organelles. Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes. Eukaryotic cells are more complex. They contain a nucleus — a membrane-enclosed compartment that houses the cell's DNA — as well as a variety of specialised organelles. Animals, plants, fungi, and protists are all made of eukaryotic cells.

Within a eukaryotic cell, different organelles perform specific functions. The nucleus is the control centre — it contains the cell's genetic information (DNA) and directs all cell activities. The mitochondria are the powerhouses of the cell — they produce ATP, the energy currency that powers almost all cellular processes. The ribosomes are the protein-building machines. The endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus are involved in producing and shipping proteins and other molecules.

Plant cells differ from animal cells in important ways. They have a rigid cell wall made of cellulose, a large central vacuole for storing water, and chloroplasts — the organelles where photosynthesis takes place. Photosynthesis is the process by which plants convert light energy from the sun into chemical energy stored in sugar.

Studying cells has led to breakthroughs in medicine, agriculture, and biotechnology. Understanding how cancer cells divide differently from healthy cells, how viruses hijack cellular machinery, and how genes are expressed — all begin with understanding the cell.
